Models run on this phone. Robot goes online only to download one you pick. Whichever model answers, Robot\'s cards and switches (Settings › Actions, Safety & privacy) decide what asks you first, and nothing leaves the phone unless you ask. Questions in a new conversation take longer with the slower models.

Speeds on the models\' pages are measured on a Pixel 10 Pro where they say so, otherwise estimates, each with where it comes from.

Use the GPU: on the GPU, Fast starts answering sooner, uses less battery and leaves the CPU to Robot\'s voice; the CPU may write a little faster. If the GPU fails, Robot switches to the CPU by itself and says so.

Let the model think first: some models can reason before they answer: Qwen3, MiniCPM 5, and GGUF files whose chat template allows it. On, they may: answers take longer, and the thinking is never shown or read out. Off, Robot asks them to answer directly. Robot\'s own Gemma models answer the same either way.

About the downloads: each model downloads from Hugging Face only when you tap Download, pinned to one commit of its repository; Robot checks the file\'s SHA-256 before it is ever loaded, and the download resumes by itself if the connection drops. You can also download a file on a computer and import it. Nothing you say or type goes to Hugging Face. The voice models are for talking to Robot and hearing it answer. They run on the phone; nothing you say leaves it. Each file is checked (SHA-256) before Robot uses it. Wi-Fi recommended.

A .litertlm (LiteRT-LM) or .gguf (llama.cpp) file. Robot copies it; it needs the file\'s size again in free space, plus room for a cache when LiteRT-LM runs it on the CPU (a .gguf needs none).
This build of Robot can\'t run .gguf files (its llama.cpp library wasn\'t built).
Only import a file you trust

A .litertlm file runs with Robot\'s own permissions: LiteRT-LM reads it inside Robot\'s model process, which can reach your contacts, calendar, messages, memory and the internet. Robot checks the file\'s layout first, not the model inside it, so a file made to attack LiteRT-LM could act as Robot. Only import files you trust, from their makers. (A .gguf file runs in a separate process with no permissions.)

Run this file on the TPU?
Robot\'s check says this file was compiled for the %1$s\'s TPU, which this phone has. It isn\'t Robot\'s pinned Fast model, so Robot can\'t vouch for it:
Most of it is compiled TPU code that nobody can review. It runs through the phone\'s own TPU driver and Google\'s vendor libraries, outside what Robot\'s separate model process can contain.
A bad or mismatched build can crash Robot\'s model, hang the TPU until the phone restarts, or, rarely, restart the phone.
Its SHA-256 only proves the file is the one you picked, not that it is safe.
Google\'s Tensor compiler is a closed beta whose terms forbid sharing what it builds without Google\'s permission: a TPU build not published by Google may have been shared against them.
Robot\'s cards and switches still apply, as with every model: what asks you first doesn\'t change.
A TPU build can\'t run on the CPU: without the TPU, Robot doesn\'t use it.
